text: Encryption at rest stopped being a differentiator years ago — nearly every Azure and AWS data service encrypts by default. The question that actually matters in a security engineering role is who holds the key doing that encrypting, because that determines who can decrypt the data, who can revoke access instantly, and who has to prove control over it during an audit.

There are two models. Platform-managed keys — Microsoft-managed on Azure, AWS-managed on AWS — are generated, stored, and rotated entirely inside the provider's infrastructure; you never touch them, and that's the default almost everywhere, at no extra cost. Customer-managed keys, or CMK, live in Azure Key Vault or AWS KMS instead, and you control their access policy and rotation. The real payoff is a kill switch: revoke the key, and the encrypted data becomes unreadable immediately, independent of anything the provider does.

On Azure, storage accounts default to Microsoft-managed Storage Service Encryption but can point at a Key Vault key instead; Azure SQL's Transparent Data Encryption works the same way, with an optional customer-supplied TDE protector key; and Azure Disk Encryption is customer-managed by design, storing its keys in Key Vault from the start. On AWS, S3 gives three real choices — SSE-S3 with an AWS-held key, SSE-KMS backed by an AWS-managed or customer-managed KMS key, and SSE-C where you supply the key yourself and AWS never stores it. EBS and RDS follow the same KMS-backed pattern.

Here's where engineers get tripped up: at-rest encryption being on by default does not mean in-transit encryption is enforced. Azure Storage's "Require secure transfer" setting has to be turned on to reject plain HTTP outright. S3 has no single toggle — you enforce TLS with a bucket policy statement denying any request where aws:SecureTransport is false. Skip that policy, and the bucket happily answers unencrypted requests. Treat encryption in transit as something you configure and verify, not something you assume because the service supports TLS.

So when is a customer-managed key actually worth the operational overhead of maintaining rotation policies and auditing access? When a compliance framework or contract explicitly requires independent, on-demand revocation of your own data. When you need a dedicated audit trail of every key operation, which both Key Vault and KMS log in detail. Outside those cases, a platform-managed key isn't a weaker security posture — it's the same encryption, maintained by a team whose entire job is managing keys correctly.

Next lesson goes one level deeper into the services that actually hold these keys — Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS — including how their access models differ, and how key rotation really works in each one.
